clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function variants in KCNQ1, which encodes the Kv7.1 alpha subunit carrying the slow delayed rectifier potassium current (IKs); it is the commonest genotype of congenital long QT syndrome.

IKs is the principal current recruited to shorten repolarisation during sympathetic activation, so patients characteristically fail to shorten (or paradoxically prolong) the QT interval with exercise and are prone to events during physical exertion.
Swimming and diving into cold water are near-signature triggers; a young person with syncope or a near-drowning episode while swimming should prompt consideration of LQT1.
The resting ECG typically shows a broad-based, smooth, prolonged T wave.
Beta-blockers are more protective in LQT1 than in any other subtype, and good adherence markedly reduces cardiac events.

Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) KCNQ1 variants produce Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome, combining profound congenital sensorineural deafness with a severe, markedly prolonged QT phenotype.

A substantial proportion of gene carriers have a normal or borderline resting QT interval (concealed LQT1), so genetic testing and cascade family screening remain valuable despite a non-diagnostic ECG.
Participation in competitive sport, especially swimming, warrants individualised risk assessment, supervision and precautions.
reference.pathophysiology: LQT1 arises from loss-of-function variants in KCNQ1, encoding the Kv7.1 pore-forming subunit that co-assembles with the KCNE1 (minK) accessory subunit to conduct the slow delayed rectifier potassium current, IKs. IKs activates slowly and constitutes the main repolarisation reserve recruited when heart rate rises and beta-adrenergic tone increases, being augmented by protein kinase A phosphorylation. When IKs is reduced through haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative subunit interactions, the ventricular action potential fails to shorten appropriately during sympathetic surges; the QT interval lengthens rather than adapts, transmural dispersion of repolarisation widens, and early afterdepolarisations can trigger torsades de pointes. This mechanism explains the strong adrenergic and exertional trigger profile. Inheritance is autosomal dominant in Romano-Ward syndrome; because Kv7.1/IKs also drives endolymph production in the stria vascularis of the inner ear, biallelic loss of function causes the Jervell and Lange-Nielsen phenotype of congenital deafness with severe QT prolongation.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital long QT subtypes, particularly LQT2 and LQT3
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (exertional events with a normal resting QT)
Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome when congenital deafness coexists
Structural causes of exertional syncope such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
additionalInvestigations: Twelve-lead ECG with QT interval measurement and T-wave morphology assessment
Exercise stress testing examining QT adaptation, looking for failure to shorten or paradoxical prolongation during recovery
Targeted or panel genetic testing including KCNQ1, with cascade screening of relatives
Serum electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium
Audiological assessment when biallelic disease or deafness is suspected
Adrenaline (catecholamine) provocation testing in selected diagnostic uncertainty
redFlags: Syncope or seizure-like collapse during exertion, particularly while swimming
Documented torsades de pointes or aborted cardiac arrest
Family history of sudden unexplained death, drowning, or sudden infant death
Very marked QT prolongation or T-wave alternans on the ECG
reference.prognosis: With beta-blocker therapy and avoidance of exertional and adrenergic triggers the prognosis is generally favourable, and per-event lethality is lower than in LQT3. Residual risk rises with greater QT prolongation, prior syncope, young age at first event and poor treatment adherence.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal resting QT excludes disease, when concealed LQT1 is common
Failing to recognise swimming-related syncope as a hallmark warning sign
Discontinuing beta-blockers or introducing QT-prolonging medicines
Overlooking audiological review and biallelic testing when deafness coexists
Relying on a resting ECG alone and missing failure of QT shortening on exercise
references: International inherited arrhythmia / long QT syndrome consensus guidelines
management: Establish beta-blockade with a non-selective agent such as nadolol or propranolol as first-line therapy, more protective in this subtype than any other, and stress strict adherence
Advise avoidance of unsupervised swimming and diving and modification of strenuous or competitive exertion, the characteristic triggers
Correct and maintain potassium, magnesium and calcium, and avoid QT-prolonging drugs lifelong
Treat acute torsades de pointes with intravenous magnesium and electrolyte correction, and defibrillate sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or arrest
Add left cardiac sympathetic denervation or an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for breakthrough events, prior arrest or high-risk features despite beta-blockade
Offer targeted genetic testing of KCNQ1 with cascade screening of relatives, and assess for biallelic Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome with audiological evaluation
Manage through an inherited cardiac conditions service and escalate for syncope, documented arrhythmia or poor treatment response
